analysis.one_liner: Cancels 2019 regulatory rollbacks and restores stronger protections for endangered and threatened species.
analysis.headline: The House committee reported the bill on a 21-16 vote and it was placed on a waiting list for the floor, but no vote ever came before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would throw out three rules the Interior and Commerce Departments issued in 2019 that loosened how the Endangered Species Act is enforced. Under the restored rules, threatened species automatically get the same protections as endangered ones, agencies have to consult more often with federal wildlife scientists before approving projects, and economic assessments cannot be used when deciding whether a species should be listed [S2][S3][S4]. The bill never reached a vote in either chamber and died when the Congress ended [S1][S6].
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday people who use public lands, fish, hunt, or value wildlife: threatened species regain automatic full protections, habitat designations get stronger, and federal wildlife scientists regain their formal gatekeeping role before projects go forward [S2][S3]. Future generations benefit from species kept off the extinction list.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the long-standing rule that threatened species automatically receive the same legal protections as endangered species, which the 2019 rules had made case-by-case [S2][S3].

Reinforces the requirement that federal agencies consult with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or National Marine Fisheries Service scientists before taking actions that could harm listed species or their habitats [S2][S3].
Bars economic assessments from influencing decisions on whether a species gets listed, returning listings to the scientific standard [S2][S3].
Restores the stricter criteria for designating critical habitat, the land that listed species need to recover [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and mining companies and real estate developers whose projects sit in or near protected habitat. They would face more mandatory wildlife consultations, potentially stricter habitat designations, and longer permitting timelines — which is the point of the bill [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill is a blunt restore-and-repeal: rather than writing new rules, it simply voids the 2019 updates and reinstates the old ones, including procedures that critics said were slower and less flexible [S4].

Prohibiting economic assessments in listing decisions means blanket restrictions can be imposed without weighing the compliance costs to property owners, businesses, and local governments, a tradeoff supporters accept to keep listings scientific [S2][S3].
Stronger consultation and habitat rules can delay or constrain infrastructure, housing, and energy projects in habitat areas, raising costs that can ultimately be passed to consumers and taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is honest: stronger species protections slow down and raise the cost of development in habitat areas, and this bill accepts that cost to prevent irreversible extinctions. The cost is real but concentrated; the benefit — functioning ecosystems and species recovery — is broad and long-term. The bill's weakness is design, not purpose: it reverts to decades-old rules rather than updating them, leaving the underlying law open to the same cycle of rollback and restoration every time administrations change.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee passed it out on a 21-16 vote and put it on the list of bills ready for the floor, but the House never voted and the Senate never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on September 17, 2019, to nullify the three 2019 Endangered Species Act rules issued by the Interior and Commerce Departments [S1][S6].
It was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and its Water, Oceans, and Wildlife subcommittee, which held a hearing on September 24, 2019 [S6].
The full committee ordered the bill reported on January 29, 2020, by a vote of 21 to 16, and formally reported it on August 7, 2020, with House Report 116-469 [S6].
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills eligible for a House floor vote — but no floor vote was ever scheduled [S6].
128 House Democrats, all members of that party, had cosponsored the bill [S5].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without a vote in either chamber [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The industries that benefit from the looser 2019 rules — energy developers, mining companies, and land developers — kept the weaker habitat and consultation requirements because the bill never became law. Species and the people who depend on public lands got no relief from the rollbacks.

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-AZ) and Chair, House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and moved it through his committee, which reported it on August 7, 2020.

for.name: 21 House Natural Resources Committee members
for.what_they_did: Voted 21-16 on January 29, 2020, to order the bill reported to the House.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; the Senate never considered it.

against.name: Trump administration
against.what_they_did: Issued the three 2019 rules the bill sought to void, and defended them in office as the bill sat without a vote.

against.name: 16 House Natural Resources Committee Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no when the committee ordered the bill reported, 21-16.

sides.party_line_note: All 128 cosponsors were House Democrats, the committee's report vote was 21-16 with Republicans in opposition, and no Republican ever supported it in the record.

industries.note: The 2019 rules loosened the wildlife-consultation process and critical habitat designations that constrain drilling and mining; the bill would have restored them, adding permitting friction those industries have pushed to avoid.
Stronger critical habitat criteria and automatic protections for threatened species can restrict or delay construction on habitat land, directly raising project costs.
Restored consultation requirements mean more federal wildlife review before projects can proceed, adding time and cost, though the underlying protections are science-based and predictable.
